documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: Generative AI in Teaching and Learning
documents.stance_why: The page says "The university does not have a blanket AI policy" and that "instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations", so it sets no stance itself and delegates.
documents.summary: UConn's teaching center states that the university has no blanket AI policy and that instructors set and communicate course- and assignment-level rules within data, integrity and FERPA policies. It gives syllabus-content advice, tool and privacy guidance, notes that detectors are unreliable and not licensed, and lists workshops and example approaches.

units.why: A statement that the university sets no single AI rule: "does not have a blanket AI policy". It pushes the decision down, so P04 (each instructor or assignment sets the rule) fits better than P85 because the next sentence names instructors.
units.anchor: The university does not have a blanket AI policy.

units.why: States which existing policies govern AI use: "AI use is governed by the" Data Classification Policy, the academic integrity policy and FERPA. P77 (comply with existing law and policy) since no AI-specific rule is made.
units.anchor: AI use is governed by the
units.frag_start: AI use is governed by the
units.policy: AI use is governed by the Data Classification Policy, the Academic, Scholarly, and Professional Integrity and Misconduct Policy, and the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974 (FERPA).

units.why: Assigns the rule-setting job to instructors: "instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations". This delegation defines the document's stance, so P04.
units.anchor: instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations
units.frag_start: Within that framework, instructors are responsible
units.policy: Within that framework, instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations for generative AI use.

units.why: Says "There is no single approach appropriate for every course, discipline, or assignment", justifying variation. Same delegation idea as P04; P83 and P85 do not fit because the reason is variation, not objectives or units.
units.anchor: There is no single approach appropriate for every course, discipline, or assignment.
units.fit_note: Adds the reason: no one approach suits all courses, disciplines or assignments.

units.why: Scopes what AI means: "what counts as 'using AI' is not always obvious to students", with tools from autofill and Grammarly to ChatGPT. A scope and definition point, so P61.
units.anchor: what counts as “using AI” is not always obvious to students
units.fit_note: Also notes the ambiguity for students, not only a definition.

units.why: The center recommends the syllabus address "what uses of generative AI are permitted and what uses are not, including whether that differs by assignment". A recommendation to state AI expectations in the syllabus, so P09 with should modality.
units.anchor: what uses of generative AI are permitted and what uses are not
units.frag_start: We recommend your syllabus statement address:

units.why: Recommends the syllabus say "whether any use is required, and for what purpose". A syllabus-content recommendation (P09); required AI use (P79) is only asked to be stated, not mandated.
units.anchor: whether any use is required, and for what purpose
units.fit_note: Specifically asks instructors to say whether AI use is required.

units.why: Recommends stating "what AI tools students are required to purchase or access, including any cost or account requirements". Cost and access transparency; P51 is nearest though it does not say paid tools are barred.
units.anchor: what AI tools students are required to purchase or access
units.frag_start: what AI tools students are required
units.fit_note: Only asks instructors to disclose costs and accounts; does not forbid requiring paid tools.

units.why: Recommends the syllabus state "what disclosure or acknowledgment of AI use you expect". It concerns disclosure, but as a syllabus-content recommendation to instructors rather than a student rule, so P24 with fit_note.
units.anchor: what disclosure or acknowledgment of AI use you expect
units.fit_note: Instructors are advised to state a disclosure expectation; the document itself does not require disclosure.

units.why: Recommends stating "what will happen if a student uses AI outside your stated expectations". Consequences are named only as something to communicate, so P09 not P37 (no concrete penalty).
units.anchor: what will happen if a student uses AI outside your stated expectations
units.frag_start: what will happen if a student
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to state consequences; no specific penalty is given.

units.why: Recommends the statement explain "how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn", tying AI rules to learning goals: P83.
units.anchor: how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn

units.why: Suggests instructors "tell students whether and how you use generative AI yourself" in design, feedback, assessment or communication. Instructor disclosure to students is P47; "may also want to" makes it optional.
units.anchor: tell students whether and how you use generative AI yourself
units.frag_start: You may also want to tell
units.frag_end: helps build trust and avoids misunderstandings.

units.why: The page gives as a reason "There is confusion, however, about which professors allow AI" and says students may avoid AI or misuse it. A rationale for clear rules that fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: There is confusion, however, about which professors allow AI to be used in projects
units.uncovered_note: Rationale: students are unsure which instructors allow AI and where collaboration ends and cheating begins, so they avoid or misuse it.

units.why: Cites a 2024 study: "30 percent of students reported using generative AI". Evidence on use rather than learning effects, so nearest is P55.
units.anchor: 30 percent of students reported using generative AI
units.fit_note: Evidence is about prevalence and attitudes, not effects on learning.

units.why: Says including or addressing AI "will help prepare them for jobs or further work in most disciplines". Professional-skill rationale, P44.
units.anchor: will help prepare them for jobs or further work in most disciplines

units.why: Invites instructors to contact CETL: "reach out to CETL for 1:1 consultations on integrating AI". Support for faculty, P63.
units.anchor: reach out to CETL for 1:1 consultations on integrating AI into activities and assignments

units.why: Lists the "foundations of AI literacy": when to use AI, prompting, evaluating output, concepts, and risks. Curricular AI-literacy, P70; the list also touches P31 and P93 but is offered as one framework.
units.anchor: The foundations of AI literacy are:
units.frag_start: The foundations of AI literacy are:
units.frag_end: risks in AI and AI enterprises
units.policy: The foundations of AI literacy are knowing when to use AI and when not to, knowing how to ask and refine questions with an AI chatbot, critically evaluating AI output, conceptual understanding of generative AI models and algorithms, and identification of a wide range of risks in AI and AI enterprises.

units.why: States the Microsoft contract: "It is free to faculty, staff, and students". A licensed institution-wide tool, so P92 rather than P17 (course-specific).
units.anchor: It is free to faculty, staff, and students.

units.why: Says "it is recommended, though not required, that you use Copilot" because of its protections. Recommends the licensed tool: P92, should.
units.anchor: it is recommended, though not required, that you use Copilot
units.frag_start: Due to these protections, it is recommended,

units.why: Explains the contract "affords privacy protections" and queries "will not be used to train large language models". Privacy protection of a vetted tool, P50.
units.anchor: the contract affords privacy protections and includes an agreement that queries will not
units.frag_start: In both cases, the contract affords

units.why: Tells employees to "avoid using any software, including AI platforms, for anything to do with protected university data", including FERPA data. A data protection rule, P50 (P49 is about students and course materials).
units.anchor: including AI platforms, for anything to do with protected university data
units.frag_start: all university employees should make sure

units.why: Lists a practice for choosing a tool: "Understand FERPA and follow" the Data Classification Policy. Compliance with existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: Understand FERPA and follow
units.policy: Understand FERPA and follow UConn's Data Classification Policy when deciding on and working with an AI tool.

units.why: Advises "Connect the choice to your course learning objectives" when picking a tool: P83.
units.anchor: Connect the choice to your course learning objectives

units.why: Advises instructors to "Transparently communicate to students your definition of plagiarism and cheating". Explaining rules to students; P66 rather than P09 since it is about defining misconduct, not the syllabus statement.
units.anchor: Transparently communicate to students your definition of plagiarism and cheating

units.why: Advises "Communicate to students the risks of AI". Explaining AI risks to students: P66.
units.anchor: Communicate to students the risks of AI
units.fit_note: The content to explain is the risks of AI, not the course's rules.

units.why: Advises to "Require students to demonstrate comprehension of what is 'identifiable information'" so they avoid entering it into AI. Data protection teaching, P50.
units.anchor: Require students to demonstrate comprehension of what is “identifiable information”

units.why: Says "detection software is of limited use and may be detrimental" because of false positives. Detectors are unreliable: P39.
units.anchor: detection software is of limited use and may be detrimental

units.why: States "UConn does not currently license any AI detection software". An institutional decision not to use detectors, P39.
units.anchor: UConn does not currently license any AI detection software
units.frag_start: As such, UConn does not currently license

units.why: Says "CETL continues to review and evaluate them" (detectors). Ongoing review of detection tools, P54.
units.anchor: CETL continues to review and evaluate them
units.frag_start: Still, this technology continues to develop

units.why: Advises to "Require students to slow down, engage as active readers, and reflect on their engagement with these tools", with a template to track AI use. Reflection on AI use is P26; it is a suggestion to instructors.
units.anchor: Require students to slow down, engage as active readers, and reflect on their engagement
units.frag_start: Using an AI chatbot can feel natural
units.fit_note: Framed as a pedagogical reflection, with points suggested, rather than disclosure for integrity.

units.why: Describes the "AI marble layer cake" approach that "incorporates AI into both homework and in-class work" with class analysis of outputs. A course design built around AI: P35.
units.anchor: incorporates AI into both homework and in-class work
units.frag_end: students got when they did the homework.

units.why: Describes the "AI sandwich": "students use AI as a brainstorming partner first", then human work, then AI as writing partner. Nearest P15 (brainstorming) but it also stages the sequence.
units.anchor: students use AI as a brainstorming partner first
units.frag_start: The very simple idea behind this approach
units.fit_note: Also prescribes a sequence: AI brainstorm, human collaboration, then AI as writing partner.

units.why: Points instructors to the Office of Community Standards, which "offers information on handling plagiarism and cheating". Referral to the integrity office; P36 nearest.
units.anchor: offers information on handling plagiarism and cheating
units.fit_note: Only refers instructors to the integrity office; does not classify AI misuse itself.

units.why: Observes "cheating and plagiarism often stem from reasons other than lack of ethics", e.g. unclear collaboration norms, overload. A good-faith, non-punitive framing: P68.
units.anchor: cheating and plagiarism often stem from reasons other than lack of ethics
units.frag_start: While safeguarding the integrity of assessment
units.fit_note: Gives reasons for misconduct rather than prescribing an educative response.

units.why: Says "There is a lot we can do, pedagogically, to scaffold assignments, make content accessible". Easing the causes of misuse: P99.
units.anchor: There is a lot we can do, pedagogically, to scaffold assignments, make content accessible
units.frag_start: There is a lot we can do,

units.why: Asks to "communicate the value and purpose of using generative AI critically and judiciously". Explaining the purpose to students: P66.
units.anchor: communicate the value and purpose of using generative AI critically and judiciously
units.frag_start: There is a lot we can do,

units.why: Says the University Senate and Provost "maintain guidelines for academic integrity and scholastic standards". Names who owns integrity guidelines: P80.
units.anchor: maintain guidelines for academic integrity and scholastic standards
units.frag_start: UConn’s University Senate, and the Office

units.why: Says AI benefits and challenges "will be realized within departments and shaped by disciplinary norms". Pushes AI practice to local units: P85 is nearest.
units.anchor: shaped by disciplinary norms of inquiry, accreditation requirements, and local curricula
units.fit_note: Says impacts are shaped locally, not that departments may set rules.

units.why: States "The resources on this page will be updated continuously". The page is provisional: P54.
units.anchor: The resources on this page will be updated continuously.

units.why: CETL "organizes learning communities and workshops" for faculty, staff and students including help with syllabus policies. Training for the community (not faculty only): P70.
units.anchor: CETL organizes learning communities and workshops where UConn faculty, staff and students can gain awareness

units.why: A workshop is announced on helping "students effectively prompt generative AI for homework tutoring" via "tutor prompts". AI as homework tutor under guidance: P12.
units.anchor: tutor prompts and “AI interviewing” protocols can be integrated into homework assignments
units.fit_note: Also includes structured prompt protocols integrated in homework.

units.why: A workshop description says the "Blackboard AI Design Assistant can simplify course development". Instructor AI use in course work: P59.
units.anchor: Learn how the Blackboard AI Design Assistant can simplify course development
units.frag_start: Learn how the Blackboard AI Design

units.why: Describes a faculty-run "aggressively AI inclusive policy" in an instructor's courses. An example of permit-by-default, P02, reported as an event.
units.anchor: aggressively AI inclusive policy he
units.frag_start: will facilitate a discussion of the
units.fit_note: Reported as a workshop topic; the policy's content is not given.

notes: Only one included document (CETL page). Large parts are workshop listings and external resource links, coded only where they state guidance. Computing and school layers: none found.
